Where it began

Chaminda Vaas was born on 27 January 1974 and grew up in Mattumagala, a village near Wattala on the edge of Colombo. He went to St. Anthony's College in Wattala for his first years of school and then to St. Joseph's College in Colombo, a school famous for its cricketers.

After school he joined Colts Cricket Club, and he was only 16 when he played his first first-class match, against Galle in December 1990. Nearly four years later he was in the Test side.

The player

He first played Test cricket in August 1994, against Pakistan at Kandy. Within a year he had bowled Sri Lanka to their first Test win abroad, taking five wickets in each innings at Napier against New Zealand, and he was player of the match again in the next Test at Dunedin. He played every game of the 1996 World Cup, including the final, as Sri Lanka became world champions.

In 111 Tests between 1994 and 2009 he took 355 wickets at 29.58, with 12 five-wicket innings, two ten-wicket matches and a best of 7 for 71. He also made 3,089 runs. In one-day cricket he became only the fourth bowler to reach 400 wickets, and his 8 for 19 against Zimbabwe in December 2001 was the first eight-wicket haul the format had seen.

What made him special

He was a left-arm swing bowler of great accuracy who almost never gave the batsman anything easy. Early on he had real pace, and as it faded he added an inswinger, a well-hidden off-cutter and reverse swing. That kind of skill took wickets on the dry, dusty pitches of the subcontinent, which are usually kind only to spinners. With Muttiah Muralitharan at the other end he formed one of the most productive bowling partnerships the game has seen.

His batting took its time to blossom. He waited until his 97th Test for his first hundred, an unbeaten 100 against Bangladesh at Colombo in 2007, which was a record wait at the time. It was worth it.

Away from the middle

He went on to coach, working with New Zealand's fast bowlers, Ireland and, over several spells, Sri Lanka. He also played county cricket for Middlesex and Northamptonshire, where he was player of the season in 2011. Sri Lanka gave him the Deshabandu honour in 1996 after the World Cup win, and in 2015 MCC made him an honorary life member. A schools match between St. Joseph's and St. Anthony's College, Kandy, is played for the Murali-Vaas Trophy.

And finally

His full name, Warnakulasuriya Patabendige Ushantha Joseph Chaminda Vaas, is one of the longest in cricket. Scorers everywhere must have been relieved that he was happy to be called Vaas.
